clue.text: One may gripe without practical experience. (Doesn't stand to reason, negatively–something like a Monday morning quarterback.)

definitions.text: One may gripe without practical experience

parts.note: someone who doesn't stand sits, and an armchair is where they sit
a critic is one who reasons in a fault-finding, negative way

explanation.surface: A grumbler with no hands-on knowledge, likened to the fan who second-guesses Sunday's football game on Monday.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis is a second, cryptic hint: the seat for one who doesn't stand, then one who reasons negatively. A Monday morning quarterback is the American image for the same person.
explanation.definitionFit: An armchair critic finds fault from the comfort of home, with no real experience of the thing being judged.

clue.text: Anything goes in the bailiwicks of Venus and Mars!

definitions.text: Anything goes in the bailiwicks of Venus and Mars!

parts.words: Anything goes in the bailiwicks of Venus and Mars
parts.note: Venus is the goddess of love and Mars the god of war, so their domains are the two fields where the proverb says no rule applies

explanation.walkthrough: Read the two gods as their domains and 'Anything goes' as the proverb's claim that no rules apply there.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says that in romance and in combat any tactic is permitted, which is what 'anything goes' expresses.

clue.text: A large number spoken in what could be a very ethical principle.

definitions.text: what could be a very ethical principle

indicators.note: spoken tells us to take the word for a greater number by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: more is a greater number of things
L is the standard abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Somebody talking about a big figure within some lofty ethical code.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoken' says to take 'more' (a greater number) by its sound, giving MOR; then A and L (large) follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A moral is a principle of right conduct, the lesson about ethics that a story teaches.

clue.text: Eaves, possibly, but they don't offer you much of a welcome after a night on the town.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: eaves are an example of things that hang over a wall, overhangs

definitions.text: they don't offer you much of a welcome after a night on the town
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the headaches and nausea that follow heavy drinking

explanation.surface: The roof edge of a house gives a poor welcome to someone stumbling home after a night out.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the word as HANG-OVERS, things that hang over, as eaves do.
explanation.definitionFit: Eaves project beyond a wall, and the morning-after illness from drinking shares the same word.

clue.text: Form of a chemical element–and I thus take in too much refreshment with it!

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
to tope is to drink alcohol to excess

explanation.surface: A chemist toasting a newly found element by drinking too much.
explanation.walkthrough: TOPE is an old verb for heavy drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: Isotopes are variants of one element whose atoms differ in their number of neutrons.

clue.text: See 1
There's nothing in film caused by oxidation, but it's a way to get someone out of bed.

indicators.note: in places the letter for nothing inside the word for the oxidised film

parts.note: rust is the reddish coating formed when iron oxidises
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A sentence about a rust-free coating that turns into a tip for waking a sleeper.
explanation.definitionFit: To roust is to rouse someone roughly, especially to drag them up from sleep.

clue.text: Disrobing and starting to fly.

definitions.meaning: second meaning: an aircraft ... leaves the ground

explanation.surface: Someone undressing and leaving the ground, perhaps in a dream.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers both removing clothing and an aircraft's departure from the runway.

clue.text: Automobile on the curve–perhaps hugging such.

definitions.note: the answer is a noun naming a hug, so 'hugging such' points at it loosely

parts.note: a car is an automobile
an ess is an S-shaped curve, named after the letter

explanation.surface: A car rounding a bend, perhaps hugging the curve as a good car should.
explanation.walkthrough: Cars 'hug' a curve; the clue turns that phrase into the gentle touch the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: A caress is a tender stroke or embrace, a form of affectionate hugging.

clue.text: A short month comes up in one, so go along with the suggestion.

indicators.note: in places the turned-round month inside the word for one

parts.note: an ace is the one in a pack of cards

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: DEC is the short form of December

explanation.surface: A brief month arriving, so someone agrees to a plan.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'comes up' means read upwards, so the short December becomes CED; 'in' then sets that within the card that counts as one.
explanation.definitionFit: To accede is to agree or consent to a proposal.

clue.text: A magnificent character, a number otherwise at a different zone.

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
or means otherwise, as in 'hurry, or else'

indicators.note: a different zone is the same letters in another order

explanation.surface: A grand figure, some number moved to another region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges ZONE into ENZO; 'at' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorenzo de' Medici, ruler of Florence, was known as Lorenzo the Magnificent.

clue.text: One hears it's the guy who throws you out, but it's only part of the game.

indicators.note: One hears signals that the word for a thrower is taken by its sound

parts.words: the guy who throws you out
parts.note: a chucker is one who chucks, or throws, someone out

explanation.surface: A bouncer who ejects you is just part of the game, it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: A chukker is one of the timed periods into which a polo match is divided.

clue.text: A mixture of oil–or part of the book that talks about it.

definitions.text: part of the book that talks about it

indicators.note: a mixture of the letters jumbles them into a new order

explanation.surface: An oily blend, or a section of a manual on oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A mixture of oil' looks like a blend of oils, but the fodder is the two words OF OIL.
explanation.definitionFit: A folio is a leaf or page of a book, so the page that discusses the oil.

clue.text: Implicit meanings from obvious people?

parts.note: overt means open and obvious
ones means people, as in 'loved ones'

explanation.surface: Hidden messages coming from people who are plainly visible.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that implicit meanings come from 'obvious people', the opposite of hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: Overtones are suggestions or associations carried beyond the literal sense, implied rather than stated.

clue.text: Paper children?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an edition of a newspaper or magazine

explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper children' suggests cut-out dolls; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: One word names both a publication's edition and a person's offspring in legal language.

clue.text: Involved in the football procedure, with the leg commonly coming up in such bad crimes.

indicators.note: in places the reversed slang leg inside the rearranged crimes
bad crimes are crimes gone wrong, so the letters are jumbled
in a down clue, coming up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: gam is common slang for a leg

explanation.surface: Some bad offences somehow tied up with a football play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' scrambles the crimes into SCRIME; 'coming up' turns the American slang leg into MAG, since a down answer is read upwards, and 'in' sets it among those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In American football the scrimmage is the play that starts from the line where the ball is put into action.

clue.text: People enter the office because of it.

definitions.text: People enter the office because of it.

parts.words: People enter the office because of it
parts.note: office here means public office, which people win by votes rather than walking in through a door

explanation.walkthrough: The office sounds like a workplace one walks into each morning, but it is a public post won by vote.
explanation.definitionFit: Winning a vote is how candidates take up a public position, so the poll is the reason they hold it.

clue.text: Bon mot set randomly on this for one who is not quick.

definitions.text: this for one who is not quick

indicators.note: set randomly means the letters are placed in no fixed order

explanation.surface: A witty remark placed carelessly on a slow person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quick' is the old word for alive, as in 'the quick and the dead'; a bon mot set randomly on this is an epitaph.
explanation.definitionFit: A grave marker stands over someone who has died, the opposite of the quick, meaning living.

clue.text: Such men have suffered a personal loss, with an important point showing when I would shortly get worse, perhaps.

definitions.text: Such men have suffered a personal loss

parts.note: W, west, is one of the cardinal points of the compass
I'd is the short form of I would

indicators.note: perhaps indicates the word worse may be put another way

explanation.surface: Bereaved men whose situation, someone fears, could only deteriorate.
explanation.walkthrough: The cardinal compass point W, then I'D, then 'perhaps' rearranges WORSE into OWERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Widowers are men whose wives have died, a personal bereavement.

clue.text: What we swing when we run–building up things to throw at each other.

definitions.text: building up things to throw at each other

parts.note: we swing our arms as we move
a race is a run against others

explanation.surface: We pump our arms as we run, while rivals stockpile things to hurl.
explanation.definitionFit: An arms race is nations competing to build up weapons, which are things to launch at one another.

clue.text: See 1
They're far from flag officers, despite the implication!

definitions.text: They're far from flag officers, despite the implication!

parts.words: They're far from flag officers, despite the implication
parts.note: the word is also a flag, so it sounds senior, yet these are the most junior commissioned naval officers

explanation.walkthrough: A flag officer is an admiral; the word for a flag names the lowest naval rank, the joke of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US Navy an ensign is the lowest commissioned rank, while the same word also means a flag.

clue.text: Out of uniform.

parts.note: an officer off duty wears plain civilian dress instead of the uniform, and the clue names that state

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the civilian dress itself; the clue gives the state of wearing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mufti is plain civilian clothing worn by someone who normally wears military dress.

clue.text: See 1
The wrong name at the junction does wrongly get such wormy results.

indicators.note: the wrong name is that word with its letters out of order

parts.note: a T-junction is named for the letter T

indicators.note: does done wrongly means its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A bad road sign at a crossroads makes everything go awry, infested with worms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' turns NAME into NEMA; 'wrongly' turns DOES into ODES; T stands for the junction between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Nematodes are roundworms, the creatures found in wormy soil or produce.

clue.text: Give a spit to Oliver, for example.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to turn something round, as a cook turns meat on a spit
second meaning: Oliver ... is the hero of Dickens's novel

explanation.surface: Someone spitting at young Oliver.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to turn or rotate, and Dickens's orphan bears the same word as a surname.

clue.text: Offers a kind of baglike structure to a little company, with one in an important case years ago.

definitions.text: one in an important case years ago

parts.note: a sac is a bag-shaped pouch in a plant or animal
CO is the short form of company

explanation.surface: Someone offering a pouch-like part to a small firm involved in an old legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: Sacco and Vanzetti were Italian anarchists executed in Massachusetts in 1927 after a famously disputed trial.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicola Sacco was one of the two defendants in that celebrated American murder case.

clue.text: The measure of a little bear on it?

parts.note: a cub is a young bear

explanation.surface: Measuring a bear cub sitting on top of something.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts CUB above IT.
explanation.definitionFit: A cubit is an ancient unit of length, the distance from elbow to fingertip.

clue.text: It's nothing to an automobile in a version here that might offer a sweet tune.

definitions.text: that might offer a sweet tune

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
a car is an automobile

explanation.surface: A car stereo playing a pleasant melody.
explanation.walkthrough: The ocarina is nicknamed the sweet potato for its shape, so the sweet tune is a pun.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocarina is a small egg-shaped wind instrument, played for its soft, sweet tone.

clue.text: It sounds like a better than average deal–and could be the last word!

indicators.note: the clue says outright that the purchase phrase is taken by its sound

parts.note: a good buy is a bargain

explanation.surface: A bargain that might also end the conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: Goodbye is the parting word said at the end of a conversation or visit.

clue.text: Steven gets upset by such happenings!

indicators.note: upset letters are knocked over and set down in a new order

explanation.surface: A man named Steven gets distressed by what happens around him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets upset' looks like Steven's mood, but 'upset' rearranges his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Events are things that happen, occurrences.

clue.text: Proving a call for help is about the most appropriate word–but it might be a help in case of fire.

definitions.text: it might be a help in case of fire

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the distress call goes round the superlative

parts.note: SOS is the Morse distress signal
best means most suitable

explanation.surface: An argument that a cry for help is the best word, though a fireproof material might help more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' sets the superlative inside the Morse distress call to give SBESTOS, and the clue's 'a' goes in front; 'help' serves both the call and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestos is a fire-resistant mineral fibre once used in fireproof clothing and safety curtains.
